title: Interesting Origins of Everyday Phrases
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the origins of everyday English phrases. They open with a plea for donations to Cooperative for Education and shout-outs to Daniel Murgatroyd, Worldwide Words, and Graham Arst. Topics include "on the wagon" (from water wagons used to lay dust, not the temperance pledge wagon), "the exception that proves the rule" (original medieval Latin sense versus the modern misreading), "PU" as an interjection, "bury the hatchet" (Iroquois Confederacy peace tradition and its spread to other North American tribes), "in a pickle" (Shakespeare's The Tempest, Dutch origin, Samuel Pepys), "slippery slope" as a logical fallacy, "Que sera sera" (Hitchcock's The Man Who Knew Too Much, The Barefoot Contessa motto), "begs the question" (Aristotle's petitio principii and a mistranslation), and a Jimmy Carter translation anecdote. The episode closes with a listener mail about "balls out" coming from centrifugal governors.
topics: the exception that proves the rule
The Man Who Knew Too Much

entities.name: The Man Who Knew Too Much

segments.title: Opening and housekeeping
segments.summary: Josh introduces the show and asks listeners to donate to Cooperative for Education, thanks painter Daniel Murgatroyd for an oil portrait, and shouts out Worldwide Words and Graham Arst for phrase research.

segments.title: On the wagon
segments.summary: The hosts dismiss a UK gallows-cart theory and explain that 'on the wagon' comes from water wagons, carts of undrinkable water sprayed to lay dust on dirt streets, so saying one was on the wagon meant preferring that water to whiskey. The phrase was in print by the 1900s, with a Davenport Daily Leader item noted.

segments.title: The exception that proves the rule
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck debate the modern versus original meaning of 'the exception that proves the rule.' The modern sense is an outlier that suggests the rule holds. The original medieval Latin sense, 'exceptio probat regulam,' means the exception tests or confirms the rule, and the hosts find the modern reading nonsensical when examined.
topics: the exception that proves the rule

segments.title: PU
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the interjection 'PU' used for bad smells. It stands for nothing and traces to Latin 'puteo' and a Proto-Indo-European root meaning rotten, and the OED records it from the 1950s.

segments.title: Bury the hatchet
segments.summary: The phrase is traced to a 1142 peace treaty among five Iroquois nations (Cayuga, Oneida, Mohawk, Seneca, Onondaga) that formed the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, per University of Toledo researchers. Leaders buried weapons under a white pine tree. The custom later spread to European and American treaty talks, and the phrase became common in the 1790s. Tomahawk and godjiwa are noted as alternatives.

segments.title: In a pickle
segments.summary: The phrase 'in a pickle' meaning a tight spot is traced to Shakespeare's The Tempest, where Trinculo's line draws on a Dutch phrase, 'in pickle zitten.' Samuel Pepys's 1660 diary use reflects the sense of a bad state, which evolved into the modern meaning.

segments.title: Slippery slope
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the slippery slope argument as a logical fallacy. They note its 19th-century use, its frequent misuse in political arguments with extreme predictions, and James Graft's 2013 critique in The Week.

segments.title: Que sera sera
segments.summary: Que sera sera is traced to the family motto 'Che sarà sarà' of the Earl of Bedford, used in Joseph Mankiewicz's The Barefoot Contessa. Jay Livingston and Ray Evans wrote the song for Hitchcock's The Man Who Knew Too Much, sung by Doris Day. The hosts note the grammatical error in the motto and Hitchcock's remark about the song.
topics: The Man Who Knew Too Much

segments.title: Begs the question
segments.summary: The hosts explain the modern misuse of 'begs the question' to mean 'raises the question.' The original sense is Aristotle's petitio principii, circular reasoning that assumes its conclusion. The Latin was mistranslated as 'request the principle,' which shaped the English idiom. The example of Superman ice cream illustrates it.

segments.title: Jimmy Carter translation anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck tells the story of Jimmy Carter's visit to Japan, where a translator rendered his anecdote so that the audience laughed hugely, with the translator saying 'President think Carter told a funny story.' The hosts briefly discuss a possible future episode on Carter.

segments.title: Listener mail: balls out
segments.summary: Listener Ben writes that 'balls out' comes from centrifugal governors on old machines, where weighted balls spin out to the sides at high speed, correcting the testicle assumption from an earlier episode about license plates.
